Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Firefighter
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Transportation (Bicycle): Bicycle, Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Vignette:
Tariq Mansour is a 37-year-old Lebanese American firefighter who has been married for nine years and has two school-aged children. He presented for psychological assessment describing a level of distress that had become, in his own words, "impossible to keep hidden anymore." His PCL-5 score of 62 places him well within the severe range, and the picture that emerged across the intake and first two sessions was one of a man whose sense of himself had been profoundly destabilized by an experience he had never anticipated and did not have a framework to understand.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Tariq began noticing the same man near his home — first outside the grocery store, then parked across from his children's school, then on the street corner he passed each morning when he rode his bicycle to the firehouse. The man never spoke to him. What made it unbearable, Tariq explained, was the deliberateness of it: the way the figure would hold eye contact just long enough before looking away, the way he seemed to know Tariq's routes and rhythms with an intimacy that felt like a violation. Over several weeks the encounters escalated — a note left under his bicycle seat, a photograph of his front door slipped beneath it, a phone call to the firehouse in which the caller said nothing and hung up. Tariq reported the situation to police, but the man was never identified, and the contact stopped as abruptly as it had begun. There was no arrest, no explanation, no closure — only silence, which Tariq found he could not trust.

In the months that followed, the bicycle became something he could not bring himself to ride. It sat in the garage where he had once kept it by the door, and he began driving to the firehouse instead, telling his wife only that the bike needed repairs. The route he had taken for six years — past the park, along the residential blocks where the man had appeared — became a stretch of road he avoided entirely, adding fifteen minutes to his commute. His wife noticed the detour but accepted his vague explanation. What he did not tell her was that riding the bicycle, or even walking those particular streets, could collapse the distance between the present and those weeks entirely, without warning. A glimpse of a man in a dark jacket standing near a parked car, or the particular quality of footsteps behind him on pavement, could return him instantly and completely to the feeling of being watched — not as a memory he could observe from a distance, but as something happening now, in his body, with full force. When he tried to describe these episodes to himself or to his wife, the words simply were not there. He knew what had occurred. He could not say it.

At the firehouse, the changes accumulated in ways that troubled him. He had always been someone his crew relied on for composure in chaotic environments, but he now found himself scanning every new building they entered for exits before anything else, cataloguing the positions of the other men on scene, watching civilian faces for something he could not name but was certain he would recognize. Loud sounds — a door slamming in the bay, the sudden activation of an alarm during a drill — produced a spike of alertness that took minutes to subside. His lieutenant had not said anything directly, but Tariq had intercepted the look exchanged between two colleagues after he flinched at a backfire in the station parking lot, and the shame of that moment sat with him for days.

What frightened Tariq most was not the hypervigilance itself but what he had come to believe it meant. He was certain that something had broken in him permanently, that the man who had ridden his bicycle to work and felt easy in his own neighborhood was gone and would not return. A firefighter, he reasoned privately, does not fall apart because someone followed him. He had walked into burning buildings. He had carried people out. The fact that this had undone him in ways those experiences had not led him to a conclusion he found deeply shameful: that he was weak, that his reactions were evidence of a mind coming apart at its seams. It was this fear — not of the stalker, but of himself — that finally brought him through the door.
